newsitem.title: PERU: INTERVIEW-Peru says Andean tariffs too malleable.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Peru says Andean tariffs too malleable.

text.p: Peruvian Industry and Trade Minister Gustavo Caillaux stood by Peru's decision to keep its distance from the Andean Pact, saying the group's tariff structure can be manipulated at will and makes fair competition impossible.

Speaking to Reuters in an interview, Caillaux said Peru made the right decision in 1992 when it suspended its participation in the pact, which includes Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela. Peru's uncertain status in the group has been a hotly argued issued among Pact members.

Caillaux also slammed Venezuelan Foreign Minister Miguel Angel Burrelli for pressing Peru to define its position in the group, and he denied the dispute is hampering the Andean Pact from melding with the Mercosur customs union. Mercosur is made up of Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, with Chile and Bolivia as associates.

The real obstacle to a Mercosur accord is the Andean Pact's common external tariff, Caillaux said, adding the system is misnamed given the slipshod way in which it is applied. "Everyone moves more or less whichever way they want," he said.
"Peru demands, before it returns or as a condition, that the rules of the game be fair, and it is on this point that we have still not reached agreement," he said.
Peru partially withdrew from the trade group five years ago citing the "incompatibility" of the Andean external tariff system with its own economic program.

The Andean Pact has five levels of tariffs ranging from zero to 20 percent, while Peru has just two -- 15 percent on 97 percent of all products and 25 percent on the rest. Peru wants a simpler tariff system put into place in the Pact.
The pact's other members have pressured Lima to take a position, and hope a decision will come at the Andean Pact summit on April 22-23 in Sucre, Bolivia.
But Caillaux denied that Peru would announce its decision in Sucre.

"If in this Sucre meeting we do not reach an agreement, which is very probable because this is more a technical than a political problem, Peru will continue to integrate itself little by little," he said.
He denied charges Lima is being "protectionist," adding it plans to reduce tariffs this year by three or four percent.
Last week, Pact negotiators failed to reach agreement regarding import tariffs Lima should adopt in the face of the existing Pact tariff structure.

Sources at the Board of the Cartagena Accord, the pact's executive body, told Reuters at a meeting last week that Peru had applied to re-enter the group gradually over eight years, a proposal that got a cold reception from other members.
Caracas reacted most harshly and gave Lima till April 22 to fully rejoin the Andean Pact.
"I hope that by the summit Peru is completely within the community, so that the community can negotiate with Mercosur," Venezuela's Burrelli said. "We're stalled by Peru's position."

"Peru's position stalls nothing," Caillaux retorted. "Peru is discussing -- what's more, it's leading because it presides over the committee (that negotiates with Mercosur) with Vice Minister Calmet, who takes the four other countries into talks with Mercosur."
Diego Calmet is Peru's vice minister of trade integration.

He said some want to make Peru out to be "the remora of the Andean Pact," but he underscored that regional integration will not be realized until the pact can overcome "the tariff distortions that exist." A remora is a fish that hitches rides on the underbellies of other fish.

The Pact's aim is to harmonize a common external tariff among its members before reaching an agreement with Mercosur in hopes of creating a free-trade zone covering 307 million consumers and nearly all of South America.
((-- Lima newsroom 511 221-2134))
